content: Laterality refers to the preference exhibited by most humans for one side of their body over the other. This phenomenon is exemplified by tendencies such as right-handedness or left-footedness. It is not exclusive to humans and can also be observed in other animals and even plants. The majority of humans are right-handed, and many also demonstrate a general right-sided preference, favoring their right eye, right foot, and right ear when required to choose between the two sides. The underlying reasons for this phenomenon remain incompletely understood. However, it is hypothesized that the left cerebral hemisphere, which controls the right side of the body, is dominant in most humans. This dominance is further supported by the fact that in approximately 90-92% of humans, the left hemisphere is responsible for language processing. Consequently, the right side of the body is often stronger and more coordinated. Cultural and social factors may also reinforce this right-sided preference. For instance, linguistic evidence reveals a bias toward right-handedness. In English, the word left originates from the Anglo-Saxon term lyft, meaning weak or useless. Similarly, the French word for left, gauche, also connotes awkwardness or tactlessness. The Latin term sinistra, from which the English word sinister is derived, also means left. Conversely, words associated with the right side often carry positive connotations. The English word right stems from the Anglo-Saxon riht, meaning straight or correct. Terms like adroit and dexterous, which signify skillfulness, are derived from the French droit and the Latin dexter, respectively. This linguistic and cultural bias is not limited to European societies. For example, Chinese characters are designed to be written by right-handed individuals, and no known culture has been predominantly left-handed. When individuals are compelled to use the hand opposite to their natural preference, this is referred to as forced laterality or forced dextrality. Research conducted by the Department of Neurology at Keele University, North Staffordshire Royal Infirmary, suggests that forced dextrality may contribute to the observed decrease in the percentage of left-handed individuals in older age groups. Ambidexterity, the ability to use both hands or both sides of the body with approximately equal proficiency, is exceedingly rare. While some individuals can perform tasks competently with both hands, they often still exhibit a preference for one side of their body. This preference may vary depending on the activity. For example, a person might use their right hand for writing but their left hand for playing racket sports or eating. This phenomenon is known as cross-dominance. Additionally, it is not uncommon for individuals who favor their right hand to prefer their left leg for activities such as kicking a ball, using a shovel, or operating control pedals. In some cases, this may be due to an innate predisposition for left-handedness that has been overridden by training for right-handedness. Statistical data on laterality reveal the following trends: 88.2% of individuals favor their right hand. 81.0% favor their right foot. 71.1% favor their right eye. 59.1% favor their right ear. 84% exhibit the same preference for both hand and foot. 61.8% exhibit the same preference for both ear and eye. Recent studies on motor and sensory control laterality have provided significant insights. It has been established that the hemisphere responsible for speech is also the dominant hemisphere for general motor control. This command hemisphere is located in either the right or left hemisphere, but never in both. Approximately 80% of individuals are left-hemispheric for speech, while the remaining 20% are right-hemispheric. Among right-handed individuals, 90% are left-hemispheric for speech, whereas only 50% of left-handed individuals are right-hemispheric for speech; the other 50% are left-hemispheric. Reaction times are shorter on the side of the body controlled by the dominant hemisphere, with the difference corresponding to the interhemispheric transfer time (IHTT). Interestingly, one in five individuals exhibits a handedness opposite to the side of their neural dominance, as determined by reaction time studies. Laterality is not unique to humans and is also observed in animals, where it is referred to as limb dominance. For example, most horse race tracks are designed to run counter-clockwise, favoring right-side dominant horses. These horses take longer strides with their right foreleg, which aids in turning left. Trainers of left-eye dominant horses may use a blinder on the left eye to encourage the horse to turn its head slightly left and take a longer stride with the right foreleg, mimicking the behavior of right-side dominant horses. Parrots often exhibit a preference for one foot when grasping objects, such as fruit during feeding, with studies suggesting that most parrots are left-footed. Polar bears typically use their left paw to kill prey. Fossil evidence from certain mastodon species indicates laterality through differences in tusk lengths.
